outcome: Since 26 January 2024, OpenAI has released (manuscript dated 4 October 2026, public with the openai/math release on about 6 October 2026) an unreviewed manuscript claiming an unconditional proof that every integer a that is not a square and not -1 has infinitely many primes p with a as a primitive root, via a lower bound of order c_a·x/(log x)^2; a third-party Lean 4 formalisation of that infinitude statement exists. No independent mathematician's assessment of that argument was found, Wikipedia (last edited 10 October 2026) still calls the conjecture unresolved, and a 21 August 2026 preprint (Murty and Naik) is conditional on a conjectured inequality.
problem_asks: (a) A universal claim over integers a that are not perfect squares and are not -1. Negative integers other than -1 (for example -2, -3) are in scope; 0 and 1 are squares and so out of scope. (b) For each such a, the set of primes p with a as a primitive root modulo p (multiplicative order of a mod p equal to p-1) is infinite. The statement asks for infinitude only. It does not ask for a count, a density, or Artin's constant, and does not restrict a to primes, to odd numbers, or to positive numbers. Primes dividing a cannot have a as a primitive root, so the question concerns primes p not dividing a.

events.what_happened: C. Hooley, 'On Artin's conjecture', J. reine angew. Math. 225 (1967). Proves Artin's asymptotic for the primes with a given primitive root, for every non-square a with a not equal to ±1, conditionally on the Generalised Riemann Hypothesis for the relevant Dedekind zeta functions. Known to me from secondary descriptions only (Wikipedia, ProofAtlas, arXiv 2505.05601). The 1967 paper itself was not opened.
events.delivers: Under GRH: the conjectured asymptotic (count about A(a)·x/log x) for every non-square a with a not equal to -1, hence infinitude for each such a. Restriction: GRH for Dedekind zeta functions of the relevant Kummer fields, as secondary sources state.
events.remains: Unconditionally, every a in the bullet remains open. Without GRH the bullet is not settled by this result.

events.direction: Cuts in favour of the conjecture, conditionally on GRH: each such a has infinitely many primes with a as a primitive root.

events.what_happened: R. Gupta and M. Ram Murty: an unconditional partial result. For three primes a, b, c, one of thirteen explicit products of powers of a, b, c is a primitive root modulo infinitely many primes (a lower-bound sieve argument). Known only from a thesis summary and search snippets; the paper itself was not opened. Sources date it 1983 (thesis summary) or 1984 (Murty's paper and an Inventiones citation).
events.delivers: Unconditional: at least one of thirteen explicit elements built from any three given primes is a primitive root for infinitely many primes. Restriction: the conclusion picks one element of a finite list built from a, b, c; it does not establish any given integer a.
events.remains: For any given a, including each of a, b, c individually, the bullet is open. The universal claim is not reached.

checked_by.who: Journal publication cited in sources (Inventiones, per a snippet; not opened)

events.doubts: The paper itself was not read. Sources disagree on the year (1983 vs 1984).
events.direction: Partial. Cuts toward infinitude for at least one element of a finite set; does not answer the bullet for a given a.

events.what_happened: D. R. Heath-Brown, 'Artin's conjecture for primitive roots', Quart. J. Math. Oxford 37 (1986) 27–38. Unconditional. At least one of 2, 3, 5 is a primitive root modulo infinitely many primes. Wikipedia also records that at most two integers a fail the conjecture. Wikipedia's partial-results section (opened) and the ProofAtlas literature list attribute these to Heath-Brown. The paper itself was not opened.
events.delivers: Unconditional: one of the three integers 2, 3, 5 has infinitely many primes with it as primitive root; at most two exceptional integers. Restriction: the theorem does not say which of 2, 3, 5 works, and does not show that any given a satisfies the conjecture.
events.remains: The bullet for every single a, including 2, 3 and 5 individually.

checked_by.who: Quarterly Journal of Mathematics (Oxford), per citation

events.direction: Partial. Unconditional, cuts toward infinitude for some element of {2, 3, 5}, leaves each a open.

events.what_happened: N. A. Carella, arXiv:1707.06517, submitted 14 Jul 2017 (later versions carry a different title; the v9 listing reads 'Densities Of Primes And Primitive Roots' per a search summary; the v14 title is 'Simple Proof of the Primitive Root Conjecture'). Claims an unconditional asymptotic formula pi_u(x) = δ(u)·li(x) + O(x(log x)^-2) for every fixed integer u with u not equal to ±1 and u not a square, with δ(u) > 0. That is the full density form, which gives infinitude. Abstract read on arXiv (opened). The v14 HTML was read through a fetch summary (see doubts).
events.revisions: v1 14 Jul 2017; v2 14 Aug 2017; v3 20 Sep 2017; v4 21 Oct 2017; v5 21 Apr 2018; v6 8 Sep 2018; v7 6 Oct 2018; v8 17 Nov 2018; v9 20 Aug 2025; v10 30 Aug 2025; v11 28 Sep 2025; v12 8 Oct 2025; v13 15 Nov 2025; v14 14 Feb 2026 (current). The v14 comment field says 'Seventeen Pages. Refined analysis of the error term.' No withdrawal notice found.
events.delivers: Claims the full density form, unconditionally, for every u with u not equal to ±1 and u not a square: count of primes p ≤ x with u as primitive root equal to δ(u)·li(x) + O(x(log x)^-2). Its class of integers matches the bullet's class exactly (non-squares other than -1).
events.remains: Nothing, if the claim holds. The bullet's infinitude is a consequence of the claimed formula.
events.time_since_posted: 9 years 3 months since v1 (14 Jul 2017); about 8 months since v14 (14 Feb 2026)
events.doubts: Read from the arXiv v14 HTML through a fetch tool that summarised the text. I did not check each point against the PDF. (1) Theorem 4.1, the finite-field power-sum bound on which the unconditional step rests, has no proof in the paper. It says 'There are many proofs of this result, consult [32], [15, Theorem 6]' and remarks only that the bound 'seems to be optimum'. (2) Lemma 3.2 (Gauss sums) is stated without proof. (3) Theorem 4.2 requires a < x = o(p), but Lemma 6.1 applies the bound to any non-primitive-root u without that restriction. (4) The argument yields O(x/(log x)^B) for arbitrary B > 1 plus O(x^(1/2+δ) log x), not the claimed O(x(log x)^-2). (5) Lemma 5.1 gives a₁ = 0.373955…, while (7.8) and Theorem 8.1 give δ(10) = 0.3773955…; the product in (7.8) evaluates to about 0.3739558. (6) Positivity of δ(u) for all admissible u is used in the contradiction but not proved. (7) The paper does not name the theorem that removes GRH from Hooley's argument. The only attribution is to Hooley. I found no journal acceptance, referee report, or expert comment in searches.
events.direction: Claims the full conjecture unconditionally, with the density formula. Cuts toward the 'yes' answer for every admissible a.

events.what_happened: A. Perucca and I. E. Shparlinski, 'Uniform bounds for the density in Artin's conjecture on primitive roots', arXiv:2401.11589, submitted 21 Jan 2024 (one version). Over a number field K, for an algebraic α, under GRH, bounds the ratio of the Artin density of α to an Artin constant A(τ). Over Q the ratio lies between 2/3 and 2. Published in Bull. London Math. Soc. (2025), DOI 10.1112/blms.70011, per a search listing (not opened).
events.revisions: v1 21 Jan 2024 only (per arXiv listing); journal version BLMS 2025 (not opened).
events.delivers: Under GRH and assuming the density is nonzero: bounds on the density ratio dens(α)/A(τ), over Q between 2/3 and 2. Says nothing unconditional about whether any given a has infinitely many such primes.
events.remains: The bullet, entirely: infinitude for each a is not established, and the density is only bounded in ratio, conditionally.

events.what_happened: S. Fan and P. Pollack, 'Counting primes with a given primitive root, uniformly', arXiv:2505.05601 (v1 8 May 2025; v2 14 Sep 2025). Under GRH: a uniform Artin–Hooley asymptotic for Π(x;g) when log x / log log 2|g| tends to infinity, and a uniform bound O(log^19(2|g|)) on the least prime p_g with g as a primitive root, for non-square g not equal to -1. Also an average result and an 'almost-primitive-root' analogue, whose hypotheses I did not confirm.
events.delivers: Under GRH only: a uniform Artin–Hooley asymptotic and a uniform bound on the least primitive-root prime. A conditional, uniform version of Hooley's theorem.
events.remains: Unconditionally, the bullet for every a. The result is a different-hypotheses version (GRH), so it does not settle the unconditional bullet.
events.direction: Conditional on GRH: cuts in favour of infinitude, under a different hypothesis. No unconditional progress.

events.what_happened: L. Goldmakher, G. Martin, P. Péringuey, 'Refinements of Artin's primitive root conjecture', arXiv:2502.19601 (26 Feb 2025, one version). Proposes conjectures on the finer distribution of the order of a mod p, of which Artin's formula is a special case. Proves them under GRH and weaker versions unconditionally. The listing shows three authors; the PDF link text says 'and 1 other authors'.
events.delivers: Under GRH: refined conjectures about the order distribution, which are different statements from the bullet. Unconditionally: weaker versions of those refined conjectures (which ones, I did not check).
events.remains: The bullet, which is not one of the refined statements.

For a finitely generated subgroup of a number field's multiplicative group, obtains results about the index mod primes lying in a given set S, without GRH, under convergence conditions on series attached to S. The abstract does not say that the classical rational problem is covered.

events.what_happened: M. Ram Murty (Queen's University) and Sunil Naik (MPIM Bonn), 'A non-abelian large sieve and Artin's primitive root conjecture', arXiv:2608.21573 (v1 21 Aug 2026; no later version on the listing I read). Abstract: 'Assuming the non-abelian large sieve inequality, we provide a proof of Artin's primitive root conjecture.' Also: 'using duality techniques, we derive unconditional results towards the conjectured non-abelian large sieve inequality.' The introduction calls the conjecture still open. The full text was read through a fetch summary.

events.what_happened: OpenAI's openai/math release (a catalogue of manuscripts from 'an unreleased internal OpenAI model', 372 families, reported as 719 or 722 manuscripts depending on source). Family 029, 'Primitive roots for every admissible integer base': main manuscript, dated in its repo folder name 4 October 2026. Claims Theorem 1.1: for every integer a that is not a square and not -1 there is c_a > 0 such that for all large x, at least c_a·x/(log x)^2 primes p in (x, 2x] have a as a primitive root. Unconditional, so infinitude for every such a including 2. Its analytic core, per the Lean statement, is a zero-free half-plane Re s > 1 − 10^-6 for Hecke L-functions over cyclotomic fields containing μ_12 (Theorem 1.2). Its sieve step uses a Type II estimate from the companion Poisson–Dirichlet manuscript (Theorem 3.1), per the Lean README. The release was public by 6 October 2026 (OpenAI post and repo commit adc7f12, per secondary sources; the openai.com page returned 403). The PDF itself could not be read by me.
events.revisions: Manuscript date 4 Oct 2026 (repo folder name; not confirmed inside the PDF). Public release by 6 Oct 2026 (repo commit adc7f12 and OpenAI post, per secondary sources). The repo history entry of 7 Oct 2026 withdraws three other manuscripts (Weil classes on split abelian eightfolds; Kuga–Satake correspondences for K3 surfaces; rational Hodge conjecture for products of K3 surfaces) and repairs 14 others. Family 029 is not named in the entries I read. Wikipedia last edited 10 Oct 2026 and describes the claim.
events.delivers: Claims, for each admissible a (non-square, not -1): at least c_a·x/(log x)^2 primes p in (x, 2x] with a as a primitive root, for all large x, where c_a and the threshold depend on a. That yields infinitude of such primes for every admissible a, including a = 2 (VibeMathed reading; the Lean target agrees). Restrictions: the bound is a lower bound, short of the predicted asymptotic by a factor of log x (VibeMathed). The route, as Persiflage reads it, uses a quasi-Riemann-type input for Dirichlet L-functions only, not Dedekind L-functions.
events.remains: The density form that Artin's conjecture predicts (count asymptotic to a constant times x/log x) for each a. The bullet asks only for infinitude, which the claim covers for all a in scope if the claim is correct.

machine_checked.note: Target.lean has no sorry and no axiom. formalization.yaml reports sorry count 0 and axioms propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound. The main theorem thm_main, the c·x/log^2 x lower bound, imports Controlled.lean and Splitting.lean, which import further modules (Construction.Results, Splitting.Counting, Hecke/Boundary, A2/Endpoint). I read those parts that the fetch tool showed and found no sorry token; Construction/Results was truncated, a delegated lemma named ArtinPrimitiveRoots.Proofs.a2_zf_top could not be located, and a Hecke/Continuation docstring says 'sorry until the A chain is done' although its body has no sorry. The whole import chain is therefore not verified sorry-free by me.

events.directly_checkable: Not a finite object. The claim is an analytic lower bound. The third-party Lean project checks the infinitude statement (see machine_checked). A human could check Theorems 1.1–1.2 and the Hecke zero-free theorem against the manuscript, which I did not read.
events.doubts: (a) Unreviewed. VibeMathed records 'Unreviewed' and 'No independent mathematician has checked this yet'. Wikipedia states that neither proof had been reviewed by the mathematical community. The release README warns that 'Some of the unformalized results could have issues'. (b) The analytic input is strong. VibeMathed calls the zero-free strip 'a very strong claim', and Theorem 1.2 is a zero-free region of width 10^-6 for cyclotomic Hecke L-functions. (c) The proof imports Theorem 3.1 of a companion manuscript (Poisson–Dirichlet law for prime predecessors, 24 Sep 2026). VibeMathed says that companion is unchecked, and the Lean README cites it rather than proving it. (d) Sources disagree on scope. VibeMathed and the Lean project read the claim as infinitude for every admissible a. Persiflage reads it as a weak form, not Hooley's asymptotic. Emergent Mind's LLM-built index labels Artin's conjecture 'Proved', which is not evidence. (e) The release's quasi-Riemann input is itself disputed in the same release: sources give zero-free constants of 7/8 (30 Sep manuscript), 11/12 (5 Oct alternate), and 47/48 (an independent 7 Oct paper). I could not reconcile which constant feeds Theorem 1.2. (f) The Lean project's record says 'agent-reviewed' and 'No independent human expert has reviewed the formalization'.
events.direction: Cuts toward the conjecture's infinitude claim: asserts a yes answer for every admissible a, including 2, 3, and 5. The bound claimed is a lower bound of order x/(log x)^2, not the predicted asymptotic.
events.object: No counterexample; this is a proof. The object is the analytic lower bound: for each non-square a with a not equal to -1, a constant c_a > 0 and a threshold X such that, for x ≥ X, at least c_a·x/(log x)^2 primes p in (x, 2x] have a as a primitive root (Theorem 1.1). It rests on a zero-free region for Hecke L-functions over cyclotomic fields (Theorem 1.2, Re s > 1 − 10^-6) and a sieve with a Type II estimate. The constant is existential in the Lean statement and not given explicitly in anything I read, so the result is non-constructive in its constants.

events.what_happened: Two manuscripts. (a) 'Primitive roots for every admissible integer base' claims that for every integer a that is neither -1 nor a square there are c_a > 0 and x_a >= 2 such that, for every real x >= x_a, at least c_a x/(log x)^2 primes p in (x, 2x) satisfy p not dividing a and ord_p(a) = p - 1 (the main theorem of the introduction; the abstract states the same). The proof (01a-reduction.tex) builds primes p = c r Q + 1 with c in {2, 4}, Q > x^0.9 prime, and every prime factor of r in (exp((log x)^0.1), exp((log x)^0.3)), in a residue class modulo M = 8 times the odd primes dividing a, chosen so that (a/p) = -1, so the index (p-1)/ord_p(a) is odd. Primes whose index has Q as a factor are discarded using a bound on the product of |a^j - 1| for j up to 2x^0.1. Primes whose index has a prime factor l dividing r are discarded by a uniform Kummer-splitting bound (stated in 01a-reduction.tex, proved in 07-splitting.tex) that rests on the Hecke zero-free theorem (Theorem 1.2). (b) 'Simultaneous primitive roots: a conditional lower bound for prime bases' proves that for any finite set of distinct positive primes q_1, ..., q_k there are at least c x/(log x)^2 primes p in (x, 2x) with p not dividing q_1...q_k and ord_p(q_i) = p - 1 for every i. It does this only under four stated Inputs (see conditional_on). Its k = 1 case is the infinitude question restricted to positive prime bases.
events.delivers: For (a), the claim answers the question yes for every integer a that is not a square and not -1: there are infinitely many primes p with a as a primitive root, since the lower bound is positive in every sufficiently large dyadic interval. The statement matches the list's. Negative bases other than -1 (for example -2, -3, -4) are in scope and covered, through the signed squarefree decomposition a = d0 t^2 in the progression lemma, with the row d0 = -1 handling negative squares, and the Kummer bound is stated for |a| > 1. Restrictions: c_a and x_a depend on a, which the text states, and no uniformity in a is claimed. The question asks only for infinitude, so the count and density in (a) go beyond what is asked. For (b), the claim gives infinitude only for positive prime bases, one or several at a time, and only conditionally on the four Inputs. It does not reach composite or negative bases.
events.remains: If (a) is correct, nothing in the question remains open: for every non-square a other than -1 there are infinitely many primes with primitive root a. Not established by either manuscript: the predicted order x/log x (the manuscripts prove x/(log x)^2 only), the density with Artin's constant, and any uniformity of c_a and x_a in a. For (b), the unconditional simultaneous case remains open, and so do all bases that are not positive primes.
events.doubts: (a) The analytic core, Theorem 1.2, has no conductor or height cutoff and one width, 10^-6, for all cyclotomic fields containing mu_12 and all finite-order Hecke characters; the text says 'the width is common to all fields and characters in the statement'. The introduction describes the standard simultaneous zero-free regions as having logarithmic width and permitting at most one simple real exceptional zero (citing Thorner-Zaman, Theorem 3.1), and presents the common width as the new step. The text does not compare it with a published result of this strength. Cyclotomic Dedekind zeta functions factor into Dirichlet L-functions, so the statement as written also covers every Dirichlet L-function. The text does not discuss that consequence. The Hecke argument is described as built 'over each fixed F' from mechanisms of the companion 'The Quasi-Riemann Hypothesis', which the introduction says treats Q(sqrt(-3)). The marked Type II estimate is imported from the Poisson-Dirichlet companion; the coefficient criterion's dependence is 'extracted' from that argument, and the introduction says the authors verify the character and frequency estimates themselves. (b) The four Inputs are hypotheses, and the text says their proofs lie in (a) and its companions, so (b) inherits the doubts in (a). The abstract's first sentence states the result without the condition, which appears only in its last sentence. The introduction counts four Inputs, but Input 2 has two parts, so there are five displayed hypotheses. Coverage: I did not read sections 02-06, the proof of Theorem 1.2, the fixed-progression construction in 12-construction.tex, or the appendix in full. A keyword search of those sections found no 'sketch' or 'left to the reader' style flags. The points above rest on the introduction, the reduction, the rough-Type II and sieve statements I read, and the Inputs of (b).; conditional on: (a) assumes no hypothesis of its own, but depends on work outside its text: (i) 'The Poisson-Dirichlet law for the prime factors of p-1', Theorem 3.1 and Lemma 5.2, for the one-sided marked Type II estimate; the text says its coefficient criterion (Lemma 10.2) extracts the coefficient dependence from that companion's argument. (ii) 'The Quasi-Riemann Hypothesis', Part I, Sections 5-7, whose coefficient reflection and additive probe the text adapts over each cyclotomic field. (iii) Dunn and Radziwill, Section 5.1 and Appendix A, for theta comparison formulas. (iv) Kazhdan and Patterson's cubic theta representation with their erratum, and Patterson's cubic theta series, for the normalization. (v) The block-sieve and rough-density forms, adapted from 'BlockPaper' (Lemmas 2.9 and 7.4), with proofs included in the text. (b) assumes four Inputs, which it attributes to (a): the uniform Hecke zero-free assertion (the same as (a)'s Theorem 1.2: no zeros of L_F(s, eta) for Re s > 1 - 10^-6, for every finite-order Hecke character of a cyclotomic field containing mu_12); the marked Type II estimate in two parts, (i) the coefficient criterion (= (a)'s Lemma 10.2) and (ii) rough-factor cancellation (= (a)'s Proposition 10.3); the block sieve (= (a)'s Lemma 11.1); and the rough-number density (= (a)'s Lemma 11.2). Its splitting proof also takes the abelian tower argument and the prime-ideal count from (a)'s Section 9, equations (9.2) and (9.5)-(9.9), as cited.
events.direction: proves infinitude for every non-square a other than -1, including negative a (a); conditional proof of infinitude for positive prime bases, simultaneously (b)

disputes.summary: Sources disagree on what family 029 proves. VibeMathed and the Lean project read it as infinitude for every admissible a, via a lower bound c_a·x/(log x)^2. An LLM-built index (Emergent Mind) labels Artin's conjecture 'Proved'. Persiflage reads the result as 'a weak form not in the correct Hooley asymptotic version'. A search summary of a Wikipedia snippet calls the result a 'density lower bound'. I read the Lean target statement and VibeMathed; I did not read the manuscript.

Two parallel unconditional claims. Carella (arXiv 2017, last revised Feb 2026) claims the full density form unconditionally for the bullet's class. OpenAI family 029 (Oct 2026) claims infinitude unconditionally for the same class. Neither the Wikipedia article (revision of 10 Oct 2026) nor any source I found mentions or adjudicates the Carella claim. I have recorded both without choosing between them.

Model naming. The release README credits 'an unreleased internal OpenAI model'. Third-party pages go further: Emergent Mind's explanatory text says it was generated by 'GPT-6 Astra Medium', and VibeMathed labels the source 'Unreleased internal OpenAI model (Vendor: OpenAI)' and the result 'AI-discovered'. Neither third-party name is the authors' account, so I did not adopt them. The authors' own account does not name a model beyond the phrase above.
Gupta–Murty's 13-element result is dated 1983 in one thesis summary and 1984 in Murty's paper and an Inventiones citation.

summary: I ran 37 web searches and about 60 fetches. The only event in the window that claims to move this bullet is OpenAI's family 029 (manuscript dated 4 October 2026, public with the openai/math release by about 6 October). It claims an unconditional lower bound c_a·x/(log x)^2 for the primes with each admissible a as primitive root, which gives infinitude for every non-square a not equal to -1, including 2. I could not read the manuscript itself: the GitHub-hosted PDFs (the main paper, the simultaneous companion, the Poisson–Dirichlet companion and the quasi-Riemann paper) came back as compressed binary through the fetch tool, and the openai.com post returned 403. So the content of the claim rests on the release README and CONTENTS entry, the Lean statement and its import modules (read through a summarising fetch tool), and third-party pages (VibeMathed, Emergent Mind, and the Persiflage blog). The Lean target matches the bullet's yes/no question exactly. Its top-level file has no sorry, but the imported chain is not fully verified by me. Human commentary is thin: Persiflage (6 and 8 Oct) says the argument is 'not particularly surprising' and reaches only a weak form, and Zvi Mowshowitz (9 Oct, LessWrong copy) says a sibling paper 'gets to the core of Artin's 1927 primitive root conjecture' without assessing it. No referee report, journal acceptance, or named expert verdict on the 029 argument was found. Wikipedia (last edited 10 Oct 2026) still calls the conjecture unresolved, and its partial-results section records the OpenAI claim as unreviewed. Before that, the record contains Hooley's 1967 conditional theorem, Gupta–Murty's 1983/84 partial result, Heath-Brown's 1986 partial result (one of 2, 3, 5 works), and Carella's 2017 unconditional claim, which was revised through February 2026 with no acceptance found. Carella's claim is not in Wikipedia's current article. Post-2024 conditional or analogue papers (Perucca–Shparlinski, Kimmel, Klurman–Shparlinski–Teräväinen, Fan–Pollack, Goldmakher–Martin–Péringuey, Sgobba, Murty–Naik) are recorded as discounted, with Murty–Naik being the only 2026 preprint that treats the full conjecture, and it is conditional on a non-abelian large sieve inequality its authors call conjectured. AI involvement: for family 029 the only authors' statement is the release-level README sentence that 'the vast majority of results were obtained with the same procedure using an unreleased internal OpenAI model', with two named exceptions that do not include 029. I recorded that as ai.systems and flagged it as release-level, not 029-specific, because I could not read the manuscript's acknowledgement or contribution text. Third-party names ('GPT-6 Astra Medium') were not adopted. The Lean formalisation used named AI coding tools (Claude Opus 5.5 in Claude Code, GPT-6 Luna and GPT-6.1 Sol in Codex, and others) for coding, not for the mathematics, so they are not in ai.systems. Close calls: (1) Event date for 029. I used the manuscript date, 4 Oct 2026, from the repo folder name, because §5.1 dates the first written argument. The first public appearance I can evidence is 6 Oct. The later pass should choose. (2) Whether 029 'delivers' the bullet. Its scope matches the bullet's yes/no question for every admissible a, but its bound is short of the predicted density asymptotic, which the bullet does not ask for. (3) Carella's 2017 claim is recorded as a full claim. Its doubts come from a summarising fetch of the HTML and need checking against the PDF. (4) Murty–Naik is recorded as conditional, not as a resolution.
competing_reading: Read as a resolution: an unconditional proof of infinitude for every admissible a, delivered in a documented release, with a Lean statement that matches the bullet and no sorry in the top-level file, so the bullet's 'yes' is established on the record and only the density form remains open. Read as not a resolution: the claim is unreviewed, rests on a strong zero-free input whose constants are disputed within the same release, relies on a companion manuscript that is unchecked, and its Lean check covers the formal statement but a chain of imports I could not verify in full. Carella's 2017 density claim has been available for nine years without an accepted check, which is evidence about how unconditional claims of this kind have fared.
what_would_settle_it: (1) A referee report, journal acceptance, or a published expert verification of the 029 main manuscript, Theorems 1.1 and 1.2. (2) A complete check that every module in the imported chain (Controlled, Splitting, Splitting/Counting, Construction/Results, Hecke/Boundary and Hecke/Continuation, A2/Endpoint, Ext/SplittingInputs and the Proofs.a2_zf_top module) contains no sorry and no axioms beyond the standard three. (3) A read of Theorem 3.1 of the Poisson–Dirichlet companion against the way 029 uses it. (4) A 029-specific statement from OpenAI on how that result was produced, from the manuscript's own acknowledgement or contribution text. (5) For Carella 2017: a referee report, an erratum, or a published rebuttal addressing Theorem 4.1 and the Lemma 6.1 hypothesis. (6) Evidence of when the 029 manuscript was first public, to settle the event date.

event.what_happened: OpenAI's openai/math release (a catalogue of manuscripts from 'an unreleased internal OpenAI model', 372 families, reported as 719 or 722 manuscripts depending on source). Family 029, 'Primitive roots for every admissible integer base': main manuscript, dated in its repo folder name 4 October 2026. Claims Theorem 1.1: for every integer a that is not a square and not -1 there is c_a > 0 such that for all large x, at least c_a·x/(log x)^2 primes p in (x, 2x] have a as a primitive root. Unconditional, so infinitude for every such a including 2. Its analytic core, per the Lean statement, is a zero-free half-plane Re s > 1 − 10^-6 for Hecke L-functions over cyclotomic fields containing μ_12 (Theorem 1.2). Its sieve step uses a Type II estimate from the companion Poisson–Dirichlet manuscript (Theorem 3.1), per the Lean README. The release was public by 6 October 2026 (OpenAI post and repo commit adc7f12, per secondary sources; the openai.com page returned 403). The PDF itself could not be read by me.
event.revisions: Manuscript date 4 Oct 2026 (repo folder name; not confirmed inside the PDF). Public release by 6 Oct 2026 (repo commit adc7f12 and OpenAI post, per secondary sources). The repo history entry of 7 Oct 2026 withdraws three other manuscripts (Weil classes on split abelian eightfolds; Kuga–Satake correspondences for K3 surfaces; rational Hodge conjecture for products of K3 surfaces) and repairs 14 others. Family 029 is not named in the entries I read. Wikipedia last edited 10 Oct 2026 and describes the claim.
event.delivers: Claims, for each admissible a (non-square, not -1): at least c_a·x/(log x)^2 primes p in (x, 2x] with a as a primitive root, for all large x, where c_a and the threshold depend on a. That yields infinitude of such primes for every admissible a, including a = 2 (VibeMathed reading; the Lean target agrees). Restrictions: the bound is a lower bound, short of the predicted asymptotic by a factor of log x (VibeMathed). The route, as Persiflage reads it, uses a quasi-Riemann-type input for Dirichlet L-functions only, not Dedekind L-functions.
event.remains: The density form that Artin's conjecture predicts (count asymptotic to a constant times x/log x) for each a. The bullet asks only for infinitude, which the claim covers for all a in scope if the claim is correct.

machine_checked.system: Lean 4 v4.34.1 with Mathlib (commit d13f23b…), third-party formalisation of the infinitude statement only
machine_checked.note: Target.lean has no sorry and no axiom. formalization.yaml reports sorry count 0 and axioms propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound. The main theorem thm_main, the c·x/log^2 x lower bound, imports Controlled.lean and Splitting.lean, which import further modules (Construction.Results, Splitting.Counting, Hecke/Boundary, A2/Endpoint). I read those parts that the fetch tool showed and found no sorry token; Construction/Results was truncated, a delegated lemma named ArtinPrimitiveRoots.Proofs.a2_zf_top could not be located, and a Hecke/Continuation docstring says 'sorry until the A chain is done' although its body has no sorry. The whole import chain is therefore not verified sorry-free by me.

event.directly_checkable: Not a finite object. The claim is an analytic lower bound. The third-party Lean project checks the infinitude statement (see machine_checked). A human could check Theorems 1.1–1.2 and the Hecke zero-free theorem against the manuscript, which I did not read.
event.doubts: (a) Unreviewed. VibeMathed records 'Unreviewed' and 'No independent mathematician has checked this yet'. Wikipedia states that neither proof had been reviewed by the mathematical community. The release README warns that 'Some of the unformalized results could have issues'. (b) The analytic input is strong. VibeMathed calls the zero-free strip 'a very strong claim', and Theorem 1.2 is a zero-free region of width 10^-6 for cyclotomic Hecke L-functions. (c) The proof imports Theorem 3.1 of a companion manuscript (Poisson–Dirichlet law for prime predecessors, 24 Sep 2026). VibeMathed says that companion is unchecked, and the Lean README cites it rather than proving it. (d) Sources disagree on scope. VibeMathed and the Lean project read the claim as infinitude for every admissible a. Persiflage reads it as a weak form, not Hooley's asymptotic. Emergent Mind's LLM-built index labels Artin's conjecture 'Proved', which is not evidence. (e) The release's quasi-Riemann input is itself disputed in the same release: sources give zero-free constants of 7/8 (30 Sep manuscript), 11/12 (5 Oct alternate), and 47/48 (an independent 7 Oct paper). I could not reconcile which constant feeds Theorem 1.2. (f) The Lean project's record says 'agent-reviewed' and 'No independent human expert has reviewed the formalization'.
event.direction: Cuts toward the conjecture's infinitude claim: asserts a yes answer for every admissible a, including 2, 3, and 5. The bound claimed is a lower bound of order x/(log x)^2, not the predicted asymptotic.
event.object: No counterexample; this is a proof. The object is the analytic lower bound: for each non-square a with a not equal to -1, a constant c_a > 0 and a threshold X such that, for x ≥ X, at least c_a·x/(log x)^2 primes p in (x, 2x] have a as a primitive root (Theorem 1.1). It rests on a zero-free region for Hecke L-functions over cyclotomic fields (Theorem 1.2, Re s > 1 − 10^-6) and a sieve with a Type II estimate. The constant is existential in the Lean statement and not given explicitly in anything I read, so the result is non-constructive in its constants.

judgement.why: The statement asks only for infinitude for every non-square a other than -1, unconditionally. So every GRH-conditional or hypothesis-conditional result (Hooley, Perucca-Shparlinski, Kimmel, Fan-Pollack, Goldmakher-Martin-Péringuey, Cherubini-Perucca, the Järviniemi papers, Murty-Naik) is a different-hypothesis variant. Gupta-Murty and Heath-Brown prove infinitude for an unspecified member of a finite set, which settles no given a, and KST is an almost-all average; I scored these as variants rather than cases, since none fixes any a. The OpenAI family-029 main claim, an unconditional c_a·x/(log x)^2 lower bound, answers the whole question as worded, and the missing density is not asked for. It is unreviewed. I rated it doubtful rather than not_credible: the analytic input is extraordinary, but no specific error has been identified and the release is a serious, documented one. openai-029-main-2026 and openai-math-029 are the same manuscript (the second was read from source and also bundles the simultaneous companion). I answered both identically. AI role is generated: the release-level README sentence credits the model, and 029 is not among the named exceptions. The Lean formalisation is scope none (formalising a claimed proof), with coding assistants only. Carella 2017 predates the snapshot and is not_credible, given nine years of silence, retitling after a long dormancy, and the concrete gaps the record lists.
judgement.doubts: openai-029-main-2026 and openai-math-029 duplicate one manuscript (dates 4 Oct folder name vs 6 Oct public). The AI attribution for 029 rests on a release-level sentence, not on a 029-specific acknowledgement. Calling Gupta-Murty, Heath-Brown and KST variant rather than case was a close call; it does not change the outcome, because both pre-date the snapshot or are dominated by the whole claim.
